summary: A complete target-level planning pass through SV.0–SV.5: native finite-family and local-density adapters, Brun/Selberg sieves, sharp and quadratic large sieves, maximal prime distribution, Maynard prime patterns, beta/Richert/Chen almost primes, joint spins and affine sieves. All routed paper targets are accounted for. Prerequisite chains terminate in pinned declarations, named supplier stages with exact requests, or explicit proof/interface gaps. Every node remains unchecked; no stage is closed and no formalisation is claimed.

nodes.title: Weighted divisibility interchange
nodes.statement: For every coefficient function c:N→R, sum_{d|P} c(d) A_d = sum_{n in A} w(n) sum_{d|gcd(P,n)} c(d).
hypotheses: s is the existing BoundingSieve: P=s.prodPrimes, A=s.support, w=s.weights, X=s.totalMass, nu=s.nu; A_d=s.multSum(d), R_d=s.rem(d), S=s.siftedSum. Divisors are positive natural divisors.
c is arbitrary; its values need not be nonnegative.
proofSteps: Expand each A_d and interchange two finite sums; retain c(d) with its sign.
For each n, divisibility by both P and n is equivalent to divisibility by gcd(P,n). Since P is nonzero and gcd(P,n) divides P, apply Nat.divisors_filter_dvd_of_dvd to identify the inner finite set.
acceptance: For P=1 this reduces to c(1) times the total support weight, including a possible weight at zero.
For P=6 the four divisor coefficients account separately for 1,2,3,6; no coprimality condition is imposed on n.

sources.match: Same finite interchange, extended to arbitrary real coefficients and the existing weighted carrier.

nodes.title: Exact Legendre sieve identity
nodes.statement: S = sum_{d|P} mu(d) A_d, where mu is the existing integer Möbius function cast to R.
hypotheses: s is the existing BoundingSieve: P=s.prodPrimes, A=s.support, w=s.weights, X=s.totalMass, nu=s.nu; A_d=s.multSum(d), R_d=s.rem(d), S=s.siftedSum. Divisors are positive natural divisors.
proofSteps: Specialize the weighted interchange to c(d)=mu(d).
The existing identity mu*zeta=1, evaluated using the existing convolution-with-zeta formula and arithmetic-function unit, gives sum_{d|r}mu(d)=1 if r=1 and zero otherwise.
Set r=gcd(P,n) and identify the existing sifted-sum indicator. This also covers n=0, since P is nonzero.
acceptance: Empty support gives zero; P=1 returns all support weight.
For support {1,...,10}, P=6 and unit weights, S=10-5-3+1=3.
For support {0,1,2,3,6}, P=6 and unit weights, S=5-3-3+2=1: zero must be excluded.

sources.match: The exact unweighted identity is specialized to the pinned weighted carrier; Kedlaya Chapter 11, Lemma 11.2 is the weighted inclusion-exclusion motivation.

nodes.title: Euler-product main term with signed remainder
nodes.statement: S = X product_{p in primeFactors(P)}(1-nu(p)) + sum_{d|P} mu(d)R_d.
hypotheses: s is the existing BoundingSieve: P=s.prodPrimes, A=s.support, w=s.weights, X=s.totalMass, nu=s.nu; A_d=s.multSum(d), R_d=s.rem(d), S=s.siftedSum. Divisors are positive natural divisors.
No sign assumption on X and no normalization X=A_1 is added.
proofSteps: Substitute A_d=nu(d)X+R_d into the exact Legendre identity, distribute the finite sum and factor out X.
Apply the existing squarefree multiplicative Euler-product identity with f=nu and n=P. Keep the remainder sum signed.
acceptance: For P=1 the identity reads A_1=X+R_1.
For P=6 the signed error is R_1-R_2-R_3+R_6.

sources.match: Use nu(d)=omega(d)/d, with multiplicativity only on coprime arguments; the pinned carrier already contains the needed data.

nodes.title: Absolute Legendre error bound
nodes.statement: |S-X product_{p in primeFactors(P)}(1-nu(p))| <= sum_{d|P}|R_d|.
hypotheses: s is the existing BoundingSieve: P=s.prodPrimes, A=s.support, w=s.weights, X=s.totalMass, nu=s.nu; A_d=s.multSum(d), R_d=s.rem(d), S=s.siftedSum. Divisors are positive natural divisors.
proofSteps: Subtract the Euler-product term in the exact identity.
Apply the triangle inequality to the finite signed sum. Every d dividing squarefree P is squarefree, so |mu(d)|=1.
Do not drop the divisor d=1 unless the additional normalization X=A_1 has actually been proved.
acceptance: With P=1, A_1=10 and X=7 the error is exactly |R_1|=3.
The right-hand side is nonnegative even when X is negative.

sources.match: Exact same remainder bound, with nonnegative real weights instead of unit weights.

nodes.title: Lower sieve coefficient inequality
nodes.statement: If c:N→R satisfies sum_{d|r} c(d) <= 1_{r=1} for every r dividing P, then sum_{d|P}c(d)A_d <= S.
hypotheses: s is the existing BoundingSieve: P=s.prodPrimes, A=s.support, w=s.weights, X=s.totalMass, nu=s.nu; A_d=s.multSum(d), R_d=s.rem(d), S=s.siftedSum. Divisors are positive natural divisors.
The displayed lower coefficient condition is required only for positive divisors r of this P, not for all naturals.
proofSteps: Apply the coefficient condition at r=gcd(P,n), which divides P.
Multiply the pointwise inequality by the nonnegative w(n), sum over the finite support and use the weighted interchange.
Use the existing coprimality-indicator presentation of S. Coefficients c may have either sign.
acceptance: c=mu on the divisors of P gives equality.
For P=1 the coefficient condition is just c(1)<=1, and the result applies to any nonnegative weight at zero.

sources.match: The source's lower coefficient condition; the proof is the same weighted interchange as for its displayed upper bound.

nodes.title: Lower main term minus absolute remainder
nodes.statement: Under the lower coefficient condition, X mainSum(c) - errSum(c) <= S, using exactly the existing mainSum and errSum.
hypotheses: s is the existing BoundingSieve: P=s.prodPrimes, A=s.support, w=s.weights, X=s.totalMass, nu=s.nu; A_d=s.multSum(d), R_d=s.rem(d), S=s.siftedSum. Divisors are positive natural divisors.
For every r dividing P, sum_{d|r}c(d)<=1_{r=1}.
proofSteps: Expand each A_d in the lower coefficient inequality and collect X sum c(d)nu(d).
For every d, c(d)R_d >= -|c(d)||R_d|. Sum this inequality and identify the existing error term.
No multiplication of an inequality by X occurs, so no nonnegativity hypothesis on X is needed.
acceptance: The zero coefficient function yields the elementary inequality 0<=S.
Choosing c=mu recovers the lower half of the absolute Legendre estimate.
Opposite coefficient signs do not permit cancellation inside errSum.

sources.locator: Section 1, p.5, (1.5) and the main/error calculation (1.7)-(1.8)
sources.match: Lower analogue of the source's upper main/error estimate, on the pinned carrier.

nodes.title: Remainder bound at a coefficient cutoff
nodes.statement: Let D be a natural number and C a nonnegative real. If c(d)=0 for every d|P with D<d, and |c(d)|<=C for d|P with d<=D, then errSum(c)<=C sum_{d|P,d<=D}|R_d|.
hypotheses: s is the existing BoundingSieve: P=s.prodPrimes, A=s.support, w=s.weights, X=s.totalMass, nu=s.nu; A_d=s.multSum(d), R_d=s.rem(d), S=s.siftedSum. Divisors are positive natural divisors.
D>=0 is an integer cutoff; the bound includes d=D.
The support and absolute-coefficient assumptions are both necessary inputs; they are stated explicitly, not packaged in a new predicate.
proofSteps: Split the divisor sum into d<=D and D<d. The latter terms vanish by the support condition.
On each remaining term multiply |c(d)|<=C by the nonnegative |R_d| and sum. Factor out C.
This is exact finite bookkeeping; a separate family estimate is required to bound the remaining sum asymptotically.
acceptance: For D=0 the supported divisor coefficients all vanish, so errSum=0.
For c(1)=1 and c(d)=0 at every other divisor, errSum=|R_1|; D=1 does not remove mass error.
If P=6, c(2)=1, c(3)=-1, other divisor coefficients zero, and R_2=R_3=1, the error equals 2, not zero.

sources.locator: Section 1, p.5, (1.8); Section 2, p.7, support condition before the quadratic-form calculation
sources.match: Extracts the explicit consequence of small coefficient support from the source error term; does not claim that SelbergSieve.level proves a remainder distribution estimate.

nodes.title: First Bonferroni lower sieve bound
nodes.statement: A_1 - sum_{p in primeFactors(P)} A_p <= S.
hypotheses: s is the existing BoundingSieve: P=s.prodPrimes, A=s.support, w=s.weights, X=s.totalMass, nu=s.nu; A_d=s.multSum(d), R_d=s.rem(d), S=s.siftedSum. Divisors are positive natural divisors.
proofSteps: For each n, let k count the sieving primes dividing n. If gcd(P,n)=1 then k=0; otherwise the existing prime-divisor existence theorem gives a prime dividing both P and n, so k>=1.
Thus 1-k<=1_{gcd(P,n)=1}. Multiply by the nonnegative weight and sum over support.
Interchange the finite prime and support sums to identify A_1 and the A_p terms.
acceptance: For P=1 there are no sieving primes, so equality holds.
For support {6}, P=6 and weight 1 at 6, the left side is -1 and S=0.
This bound can be negative; it does not imply a positive lower bound for primes or evade sieve parity.

sources.locator: Section 11.2, Lemma 11.1 and its pointwise proof; compare Heath-Brown p.5 (1.5)

nodes.title: Weighted finite-family sieve
nodes.statement: Construct s.ofFiniteFamily(A,f,w) as a BoundingSieve with support f(A), weight at n equal to Σ_{a∈A,f(a)=n}w(a), and the same prime product, density and approximate mass as s.
hypotheses: s is an existing BoundingSieve; A is a finite set of indices in any type; f maps indices to naturals; w is real-valued and nonnegative on A. No injectivity or positivity of f is assumed.
proofSteps: Use the existing BoundingSieve record, replacing only support and weights by the displayed finite image and fiber sums.
Every fiber weight is nonnegative because all its indices belong to A. Retain the template's squarefreeness and both strict prime-density bounds unchanged.

The projection and off-image API follow from the record and finite sums. For identity-family compatibility, interchange finite fibers using the existing additive fiber theorem; only observables, not unrestricted off-support weights, agree.
acceptance: All repeated labels contribute to the weight; this is not an unweighted image sieve.
The map may take the value zero. Its divisibility and survival follow the existing natural conventions.
Replacing a population does not prove that the retained X approximates its mass.

nodes.title: Sieve with arbitrary excluded residue classes
nodes.statement: Construct BoundingSieve.ofResidueClasses(A,x,w,Q,Ω,X) with prime product P, multiplicative density prodPrimeFactors(ρ), approximate mass X, support the image of L∘x on A, and weights the sums over its fibers.
hypotheses: A is a finite index set, x maps indices to integers, w is real-valued and nonnegative on A, Q is a finite set consisting of primes, Ωp is a finite subset of ZMod p for each natural p, card(Ωp)

Write ρ(p)=card(Ωp)/p, Q+= {p∈Q : Ωp is nonempty}, P=∏_{p∈Q+}p and L(b)=∏_{p∈Q,b mod p∈Ωp}p. All products are finite, with empty product 1. These are local expressions, not new carriers or functions in the blueprint.
proofSteps: Remove precisely the empty local sets to form Q+. The product P is squarefree by the existing distinct-prime product theorem.
Use the existing arithmetic function prodPrimeFactors(ρ), not a new multiplicative-extension construction. Its prime value is ρ(p), and its value at zero is zero.
For p∈Q+, nonempty Ωp gives ρ(p)>0; the properness hypothesis gives ρ(p)<1. Empty densities occur only outside P, where the carrier imposes no strict bound.
Build the existing carrier with this prime/density/mass data and apply finite-family-sieve to the label map L∘x. This supplies global nonnegativity of the fiber weights.
Verify the projection, prime-value and inactive-prime API directly. The supported divisibility and sifted-sum laws are separate promoted lemma nodes because the error theorem consumes them.
acceptance: All-empty local data are valid and give P=1. Do not impose card(Ωp)>0 on the original Q.
If a local set has card p, use full-residue-obstruction rather than forcing density 1 into this carrier.
The chosen density extension is only multiplicative on coprime inputs: at prime powers it repeats no factor. On the squarefree divisors actually used, it is exactly the product of local densities.
The natural labels record local membership, not the magnitude of the original integer samples; no linear cutoff follows.

nodes.title: Vanishing Gram row detects the zero vector
nodes.statement: For each i∈I, rᵢ=0 if and only if yᵢ=0.

nodes.title: Diagonal and off-diagonal Gram estimate
nodes.statement: If D,C≥0, ‖yᵢ‖²≤D for every i, and |⟨yᵢ,yⱼ⟩|≤C whenever i≠j, then Σᵢ|⟨x,yᵢ⟩|² ≤ ‖x‖²(D+(|I|−1)₊C), where (|I|−1)₊ is natural truncated subtraction.
hypotheses: 𝕜 is ℝ or ℂ, represented by the existing RCLike structure; E is a normed inner-product space over 𝕜. Completeness and finite dimensionality are not assumed.
I is a finite indexing type, possibly empty unless stated otherwise; y:I→E is an arbitrary indexed family. Repetitions, zero vectors and linear dependence are allowed.

proofSteps: For an index i, use the existing additive companion of mul_prod_erase to separate its diagonal term from the remaining finite row.
The diagonal norm is ‖yᵢ‖². Bound the remaining |I|−1 terms individually by C; the existing erase-cardinality identity counts them exactly.
Thus each row is bounded by D+(|I|−1)₊C, a nonnegative number. Apply bombieri-row-bound, whose empty-family case requires no index choice.

For nonempty I, division by |I| and (|I|−1)/|I|≤1 gives the normalized bound (Σᵢ|⟨x,yᵢ⟩|²)/|I|≤‖x‖²(D/|I|+C) used in Bennett–Siksek. This is routine real arithmetic, not an analytic estimate of D or C.

nodes.title: Two-point bound for circular radial bins
nodes.statement: For a δ-separated finite real family, fixed i and m∈ℕ, #{j≠i: floor(d(x_i−x_j)/δ)=m}≤2. No upper restriction on m is imposed.

Within one floor bin, each |r_j| lies in [mδ,(m+1)δ). Two representatives of the same sign therefore differ in absolute value by strictly less than δ. Zero cannot occur because j≠i and δ>0.
For j≠k, round_le applied to x_j−x_k and the integer round(x_j−x_i)−round(x_k−x_i) bounds d(x_j−x_k) by |r_j−r_k|. This contradicts separation for two distinct labels with the same sign.
Thus the map recording whether r_j<0 is injective from the bin into the two signs. Apply the native finite-cardinality inequality.
The representative of an antipode is −1/2, never +1/2. The unrestricted floor-bin statement keeps the final partial bin and exact distance 1/2; it corrects the proof coverage gap E11.

For H=1,M=0,a=(1),x=1/4 the original sum is i; this distinguishes the starting frequency M+1 from M and the positive phase from the negative phase.

nodes.title: Cardinality above the circle diameter
nodes.statement: If δ>1/2 and a finite real family is δ-separated modulo one, its indexing type has cardinality at most one.
hypotheses: Write d(t)=‖(t:UnitAddCircle)‖ using the native real circle of period one, and e(t)=(Real.fourierChar t:ℂ)=exp(2πit). These are notation, not new carriers.
Finite point families x:ι→ℝ are δ-separated when δ≤d(x_i−x_j) for all distinct labels i,j. δ>0 is explicit; no assumption that the family is nonempty.
proofSteps: Two distinct labels would have δ≤d(x_i−x_j)≤1/2 by the native half-period bound, a contradiction.
Hence all labels are equal; the finite type is empty or a singleton.
acceptance: For δ=2 a singleton is allowed, while floor(1/δ)=0.
This does not infer δ≤1/2 from a vacuous separation condition.

nodes.title: Bombieri's additive large sieve
nodes.statement: Let M∈ℤ, H∈ℕ, a:Fin H→ℂ, δ>0 and x:ι→ℝ be a finite δ-separated family modulo one. Then Σ_i|Σ_{j=0}^{H−1}a_j e((M+j+1)x_i)|²≤(H+2/δ)Σ_{j=0}^{H−1}|a_j|².
hypotheses: Write d(t)=‖(t:UnitAddCircle)‖ using the native real circle of period one, and e(t)=(Real.fourierChar t:ℂ)=exp(2πit). These are notation, not new carriers.
Finite point families x:ι→ℝ are δ-separated when δ≤d(x_i−x_j) for all distinct labels i,j. δ>0 is explicit; no assumption that the family is nonempty.
Empty coefficient and point families are allowed. No restriction δ≤1/2 or normalization of coefficients is imposed.
proofSteps: When 0<δ≤1/2, set N=floor(H/2), L=floor(1/δ), and f=intervalVector H L a. Its support is interval-support, so separated-core applies.
Use interval-phase and norm one of e(cx) to identify each original summand; interval-norm identifies the coefficient-square sum. Since 2floor(H/2)≤H, increase the nonnegative scalar bound to H+2/δ.

When δ>1/2, separation-card-small leaves at most one point. Native norm_sum_le gives |Σ_j a_j e(...)|≤Σ_j|a_j|. Squared finite Cauchy–Schwarz against the constant one gives its square at most HΣ_j|a_j|²; this is bounded by the claimed expression.
The empty point family gives zero on the left. H=0 also gives zero, so all branches include both degenerate cases.
acceptance: The theorem has the original interval length H, not the centered N.
It is Bombieri's H+2/δ constant, not the sharper H−1+1/δ large sieve and not a multiplicative-character or quadratic-symbol large sieve.

nodes.title: Circular separation of reduced fractions
nodes.statement: For natural a,b,p,q,Q with 0<p,q≤Q, a<p, b<q, gcd(a,p)=gcd(b,q)=1 and (a,p)≠(b,q), one has ‖(a/p−b/q:UnitAddCircle)‖≥1/Q².
hypotheses: Use e(t)=(Real.fourierChar t:ℂ)=exp(2πit), the existing UnitAddCircle norm, and the native DirichletCharacter ℂ q, its conductor-based IsPrimitive predicate and its inverse. There is no new Fourier, character or Farey carrier.
proofSteps: Put t=a/p−b/q and z=round(t). Since both fractions lie in [0,1), t lies strictly between −1 and 1. If t were an integer, it would therefore be zero. Equality of the rational fractions would force a=b and p=q by the native reduced-fraction uniqueness theorem, contradicting the hypothesis.
The integer D=aq−bp−zpq is consequently nonzero. Thus |D|≥1. Clear only the positive denominators p and q to obtain |t−z|=|D|/(pq)≥1/(pq).

The native circle-norm formula identifies |t−z| with the required norm. Since pq≤Q² and Q>0, reciprocal monotonicity gives the result. This argument includes wraparound, not just the linear separation of real fractions.
acceptance: The sole reduced pair with numerator zero is (0,1); the endpoint 1/1 is excluded by a<p.
0/1 and 3/4 have circle distance 1/4 although their linear distance is 3/4.
Dropping coprimality allows labels (1,2) and (2,4) at the same point.

nodes.title: Additive large sieve over reduced residues
nodes.statement: Σ_{1≤q≤Q}Σ_{u∈(Z/qZ)×}|S(val(u)/q)|² ≤ (H+2Q²)Σ_{j<H}|a_j|².
hypotheses: Use e(t)=(Real.fourierChar t:ℂ)=exp(2πit), the existing UnitAddCircle norm, and the native DirichletCharacter ℂ q, its conductor-based IsPrimitive predicate and its inverse. There is no new Fourier, character or Farey carrier.
M is any integer, H and Q are natural numbers, and a:Fin H→ℂ is arbitrary. Write n_j=M+j+1 and S(t)=Σ_{j<H}a_j e(n_j t). Empty intervals and Q=0 are permitted.
proofSteps: For Q>0 index the family by the native dependent sum of q∈Fin Q and u∈(ZMod(q+1))ˣ, assigning the real point val(u)/(q+1). Native residue bounds and unit coprimality give the hypotheses of reduced-fraction-separation.
Distinct labels give distinct reduced pairs: equal moduli and equal natural representatives imply equal residues and then equal units. Thus the family is separated by δ=Q⁻².
Apply the inherited additive_largeSieve with this positive δ. The additive companion of Finset.prod_sigma rewrites its single family sum as the displayed double sum. Substitute 2/δ=2Q².
For Q=0 the modulus indexing type is empty and the right side is nonnegative. H=0 is already admitted by the inherited theorem.
acceptance: Modulus one contributes its single unit at phase zero; it is not discarded.
The source Theorem 16.1 has H−1+Q². This node deliberately uses the weaker H+2Q² supported by the inherited additive theorem.

Apply the native standard-character formula at that integer product and the real Fourier-character formula. Rearrange scalar products in the complex exponential. This also handles negative n and nonunit u.

nodes.title: Squared norm of a primitive Dirichlet Gauss sum
nodes.statement: For a primitive Dirichlet character χ modulo q>0, |τ(χ)|²=q.
hypotheses: Use e(t)=(Real.fourierChar t:ℂ)=exp(2πit), the existing UnitAddCircle norm, and the native DirichletCharacter ℂ q, its conductor-based IsPrimitive predicate and its inverse. There is no new Fourier, character or Farey carrier.
q is a positive natural number. The finite ring ZMod q and its unit group use their native instances, including the trivial ring q=1. Write φ(q)=q.totient and τ(χ)=gaussSum χ ZMod.stdAddChar.
χ.IsPrimitive is required; χ≠1 alone is not a substitute at composite modulus.
proofSteps: Conductor invariance under inverse makes χ⁻¹ primitive. The native finite Fourier formula gives Dχ(k)=χ⁻¹(−k)τ(χ), using the unnormalized negative-phase DFT.
Apply the native DFT twice and evaluate at −1. Its inversion formula gives qχ(1)=q. Factoring constants and commuting reflection with DFT identifies the same value as χ(−1)τ(χ⁻¹)τ(χ).

The native Gauss conjugation formula gives conjugate(τ(χ))=gaussSum χ⁻¹ (stdAddChar⁻¹). The inverse additive character is its shift by −1. The native primitive shift theorem identifies this as χ(−1)τ(χ⁻¹).

Combine the two equalities and take real parts of τ(χ)conjugate(τ(χ))=q. This proves the square-norm formula without a finite-field assumption, a squarefree modulus assumption or a new Parseval theorem.
acceptance: For q=1 the unique character is primitive and its Gauss sum is 1. Treating zero as a nonunit in this trivial ring would break the statement.
The principal character modulo 4 has Gauss sum 0 and does not satisfy the conclusion.

sources.match: The source cites the norm formula; the packet supplies its complete route through pinned DFT inversion and primitive character formulas. The algebraic product and real norm were verified by temporary Lean proofs.

nodes.title: Gauss expansion of a finite character sum
nodes.statement: For primitive χ modulo q>0, τ(χ⁻¹)Σ_{j<H}a_jχ(n_j)=Σ_{u∈(Z/qZ)×}χ⁻¹(u)S(val(u)/q).
hypotheses: Use e(t)=(Real.fourierChar t:ℂ)=exp(2πit), the existing UnitAddCircle norm, and the native DirichletCharacter ℂ q, its conductor-based IsPrimitive predicate and its inverse. There is no new Fourier, character or Farey carrier.
q is a positive natural number. The finite ring ZMod q and its unit group use their native instances, including the trivial ring q=1. Write φ(q)=q.totient and τ(χ)=gaussSum χ ZMod.stdAddChar.
M is any integer, H and Q are natural numbers, and a:Fin H→ℂ is arbitrary. Write n_j=M+j+1 and S(t)=Σ_{j<H}a_j e(n_j t). Empty intervals and Q=0 are permitted.
χ.IsPrimitive; Q is unused in this single-modulus statement.
proofSteps: Apply the native primitive Gauss-shift theorem to χ⁻¹ and the residue n_j. Inversion of χ⁻¹ yields χ(n_j), even when n_j is not a unit.
Multiply the equality by a_j and sum over the finite interval. Expand the existing Gauss sum and interchange the two finite sums.
Terms indexed by nonunits vanish because χ⁻¹ vanishes there. Reindex the remaining residues by the native unit group; this is a bijection onto the unit residues.
Apply standard-character-phase at each unit and each integer n_j. Collect the inner finite sum S. Multiplication by τ avoids making an unproved nonzero-denominator cancellation.
acceptance: The coefficients can be complex, and M can be negative.
The formula must hold at nonunit frequencies. A formula proved only for gcd(n_j,q)=1 would be insufficient for an arbitrary interval.

nodes.title: Parseval identity over Dirichlet characters
nodes.statement: For arbitrary F:(ZMod q)ˣ→ℂ, Σ_{χ mod q}|Σ_u χ⁻¹(u)F(u)|²=φ(q)Σ_u|F(u)|², summing over all Dirichlet characters modulo q.
hypotheses: Use e(t)=(Real.fourierChar t:ℂ)=exp(2πit), the existing UnitAddCircle norm, and the native DirichletCharacter ℂ q, its conductor-based IsPrimitive predicate and its inverse. There is no new Fourier, character or Farey carrier.
q is a positive natural number. The finite ring ZMod q and its unit group use their native instances, including the trivial ring q=1. Write φ(q)=q.totient and τ(χ)=gaussSum χ ZMod.stdAddChar.
proofSteps: Expand each squared norm as its complex product with its conjugate. Finite interchange gives a sum over pairs u,v of F(u)conjugate(F(v)) multiplied by Σχχ⁻¹(u)χ(v).

On units the inverse-character value is χ(u⁻¹). Apply the pinned character orthogonality formula with first argument u. Complex numbers have the required roots of unity; q>0 supplies the finite residue and character instances.
Only the diagonal u=v survives, with coefficient φ(q). Units.val is injective, so equality of residues is equality of unit indices. Take real parts to obtain the exact real square-norm identity.
acceptance: For q=4 and F≡1 on the two units, the left side is 4, equal to 2·2. Using q instead of φ(q) gives the wrong normalization.
At q=1 the equality is |F(1)|²=|F(1)|²; no nontriviality of ZMod q is assumed.

sources.match: Finite energy restatement of the existing orthogonality theorem on the unit group, not a new character theory or general Fourier transform.

nodes.title: Primitive character energy at one modulus
nodes.statement: (q/φ(q))Σ_{χ primitive mod q}|Σ_{j<H}a_jχ(n_j)|² ≤ Σ_{u∈(Z/qZ)×}|S(val(u)/q)|².
hypotheses: Use e(t)=(Real.fourierChar t:ℂ)=exp(2πit), the existing UnitAddCircle norm, and the native DirichletCharacter ℂ q, its conductor-based IsPrimitive predicate and its inverse. There is no new Fourier, character or Farey carrier.
q is a positive natural number. The finite ring ZMod q and its unit group use their native instances, including the trivial ring q=1. Write φ(q)=q.totient and τ(χ)=gaussSum χ ZMod.stdAddChar.
M is any integer, H and Q are natural numbers, and a:Fin H→ℂ is arbitrary. Write n_j=M+j+1 and S(t)=Σ_{j<H}a_j e(n_j t). Empty intervals and Q=0 are permitted.
proofSteps: For each primitive χ, take squared norms of finite-gauss-expansion. The inverse is primitive, so its Gauss square norm is q. Divide by positive φ(q), obtaining the source weighted identity.
Sum these identities over the finite subset of primitive characters. On the Fourier side only, enlarge that subset to all characters, since every squared modulus is nonnegative.
Apply character-parseval to F(u)=S(val(u)/q). Cancel φ(q)>0. The arithmetic character sum itself is never extended to imprimitive χ using the primitive Gauss formula.

At modulus one both sides equal |Σ_j a_j|². H=0 gives zero.

nodes.title: Primitive-character large sieve
nodes.statement: Σ_{1≤q≤Q}(q/φ(q))Σ_{χ primitive mod q}|Σ_{j<H}a_jχ(M+j+1)|² ≤ (H+2Q²)Σ_{j<H}|a_j|².
hypotheses: Use e(t)=(Real.fourierChar t:ℂ)=exp(2πit), the existing UnitAddCircle norm, and the native DirichletCharacter ℂ q, its conductor-based IsPrimitive predicate and its inverse. There is no new Fourier, character or Farey carrier.
M is any integer, H and Q are natural numbers, and a:Fin H→ℂ is arbitrary. Write n_j=M+j+1 and S(t)=Σ_{j<H}a_j e(n_j t). Empty intervals and Q=0 are permitted.

Apply reduced-fraction-large-sieve to the resulting double sum of Fourier values. Its constant is exactly H+2Q².
When Q=0 or H=0 the appropriate sums are empty. No asymptotic range, primality of the moduli, coprimality of the frequencies, or restriction on the complex coefficients is introduced.

The theorem estimates primitive characters of every positive modulus, including nonsquarefree moduli and modulus one. It is not a quadratic-symbol or polynomial-function-field large sieve.

nodes.title: Incomplete logarithm
nodes.statement: Construct λ_V:ArithmeticFunction ℝ by λ_V(n)=Σ_{d|n,V<d}Λ(d). This is a cutoff divisor sum, not log(n/V) and not a multiplicative function.
hypotheses: U,V,N,L,M,n,m,ℓ are natural numbers. Divisors are the native positive divisor finsets; n=0 has no divisors. μ is the native integer Möbius function, Λ the native real von Mangoldt function, and log is the real logarithm with its native value at zero.
Write λ_V for incompleteLog V. All cutoffs are inclusive below and strict above. Ioc(a,b) means a<k≤b and is empty when b≤a. No positivity of U or V is needed for the finite identities.
proofSteps: Use the existing zero-preserving arithmetic-function carrier. The finite formula is zero at n=0 because the native divisor finset is empty.

For the convolution proof, let h_V(n) be Λ(n) when V<n and zero otherwise, as a local zero-preserving function. Native convolution with ζ gives λ_V=h_V*ζ by coe_mul_zeta_apply. This local abbreviation is not a new exported truncation carrier.
The source uses V=floor(x^(1/5)); natural V keeps every endpoint exact and admits independent U,V. Its subtraction formula is established by the next lemma.
acceptance: Keep every prime-power divisor, not just prime divisors.
At V=0 the result is the full logarithm, while λ_V(n)=0 for n≤V.

nodes.title: Weighted Vaughan identity on a finite hyperbola
nodes.statement: For arbitrary w:ℕ→ℂ, Σ_{n∈Ioc(0,N)}Λ(n)w(n)=Σ_{n∈Ioc(0,min(N,V))}Λ(n)w(n)+Σ_{m∈Ioc(0,N)}μ(m)Σ_{ℓ∈Ioc(0,⌊N/m⌋)}λ_V(ℓ)w(mℓ). Real and integer coefficients are cast to ℂ.

For the convolution part expand mul_apply. At 0<n≤N rewrite n.divisorsAntidiagonal as the filtered product Ioc(0,N)×Ioc(0,N), using the native divisor-antidiagonal theorem.

nodes.title: Finite Type I–Type II Vaughan decomposition
nodes.statement: Put B=⌊N/(V+1)⌋. For arbitrary w:ℕ→ℂ, Σ_{0<n≤N}Λ(n)w(n)=Σ_{0<n≤min(N,V)}Λ(n)w(n)+Σ_{0<m≤min(U,B)}μ(m)Σ_{V<ℓ≤⌊N/m⌋}λ_V(ℓ)w(mℓ)+Σ_{U<m≤B}μ(m)Σ_{V<ℓ≤⌊N/m⌋}λ_V(ℓ)w(mℓ).
hypotheses: U,V,N,L,M,n,m,ℓ are natural numbers. Divisors are the native positive divisor finsets; n=0 has no divisors. μ is the native integer Möbius function, Λ the native real von Mangoldt function, and log is the real logarithm with its native value at zero.
Write λ_V for incompleteLog V. All cutoffs are inclusive below and strict above. Ioc(a,b) means a<k≤b and is empty when b≤a. No positivity of U or V is needed for the finite identities.

Partition Ioc(0,B) into Ioc(0,min(U,B)) and Ioc(U,B). These sets are disjoint and cover even if U>B. Distribute the finite sum.

The first block is the small-Möbius-factor Type I contribution; the second is a bilinear sum with both factors above their cutoffs. Its inner upper limit remains dependent on m. Turning this hyperbola into independent rectangles requires a separate analytic argument, not an equality asserted here.

nodes.title: Primitive character energy on a dyadic band
nodes.statement: Σ_{P<q≤2P}φ(q)⁻¹Σχ*|Aχ|² ≤ ((H+8P²)/P)E_a.

hypotheses: M,N are arbitrary integers; H,K are natural interval lengths; a:Fin H→ℂ and b:Fin K→ℂ are arbitrary. Write Aχ=Σ_{j<H}a_jχ(M+j+1), Bχ=Σ_{j<K}b_jχ(N+j+1), E_a=Σ|a_j|² and E_b=Σ|b_j|². Character values use the native residue cast.

nodes.title: Finite sum of the bilinear dyadic coefficients
nodes.statement: For real R>0, H,K≥0 and natural J, put P_i=R2^i. Then Σ_{i<J}√(H+8P_i²)√(K+8P_i²)/P_i ≤ 9R(2^J−1)+3J(√H+√K)+(2/R)(1−2^(−J))√H√K.
hypotheses: R is a positive real number; H and K are nonnegative real numbers; J is natural, including zero. The reciprocal power is 2^(−J)=(1/2)^J, never natural subtraction in an exponent.
proofSteps: For any P>0 and X≥0, square the nonnegative proposed upper bound √X+3P to prove √(X+8P²)≤√X+3P. This is deliberately weaker than using √8.
Multiply the two bounds and divide by P. The result is at most 9P+3(√H+√K)+√H√K/P.
Sum the first and last terms using the existing finite geometric-sum formula with ratios 2 and 1/2: ΣP_i=R(2^J−1) and Σ1/P_i=(2/R)(1−(1/2)^J).
The middle term does not decay with i and contributes exactly 3J(√H+√K). Retain this factor; dropping it is not justified by the block estimates. All expressions vanish at J=0.
acceptance: At H=K=0, R=2,J=3 the left side is 112; the displayed upper bound is 126.
At J=0 both sides are zero.
The scale-independent sum over four bands is four times its summand, not once.

nodes.title: Level of distribution of the primes (Maynard (1.3))
nodes.statement: For real θ the primes have level of distribution θ if, for every A>0, Σ_{1≤q≤x^θ} max_{(a,q)=1} |π(x;q,a) − π(x)/φ(q)| = O_A(x/(log x)^A) as x→∞. Here π(x;q,a) counts the primes p≤x with p≡a (mod q), π(x) counts all primes p≤x and φ is Euler's function. The Elliott–Halberstam conjecture is the statement that the primes have level of distribution θ for every θ<1.
hypotheses: x is real; q runs over the integers 1≤q≤⌊x^θ⌋ and a over the reduced residues 0≤a<q. The term q=1 vanishes identically.
The comparison term is π(x)/φ(q), counting all primes up to x, exactly as in Maynard (1.3). His footnote 1 notes that other authors use slightly different definitions; this node fixes (1.3).
Elliott–Halberstam is a named hypothesis. No node of this roadmap asserts it, and every consumer carries it as an explicit hypothesis (RS-07).
proofSteps: Define π(x;q,a) as the number of primes p≤⌊x⌋ with p≡a (mod q), the discrepancy as the supremum over reduced residues a<q of |π(x;q,a) − π(x)/φ(q)|, and PrimesHaveLevel θ as the family of big-O statements along x→∞ indexed by A>0.

Define windowError(N,q) = 1 + sup_{(a,q)=1} |#{N≤n<2N : n prime, n≡a} − #{N≤n<2N : n prime}/φ(q)|, which is Maynard's E(N,q) of (5.16). The window API follows from the level estimates at x=2N−1 and x=N−1, since windowError(N,q) ≤ 1 + discrepancy(2N−1,q) + discrepancy(N−1,q), together with Σ_{q≤N^θ′}1 ≤ N^θ′ for θ′<θ<1.
Monotonicity in θ: for x≥1 the sum over q≤x^θ′ is a subsum of the sum over q≤x^θ, and every term is nonnegative. For θ≤0 only q=1 can occur.
acceptance: The level is a statement for every A>0, with an implied constant depending on A. It is not a single-A bound.
Levels θ>1 fail (non-example test), so the Elliott–Halberstam range θ<1 is the natural limit. The Friedlander–Granville obstruction that Maynard mentions (p. 384) is not planned here.

nodes.title: Bombieri–Vinogradov: every level θ<1/2
nodes.statement: For every θ<1/2 the primes have level of distribution θ in the sense of Maynard (1.3).
hypotheses: The input is the ψ-form Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem, Kedlaya Theorem 18.4: for every A>0 there are c(A) and B(A) with Σ_{N≤Q} max_{m∈(ℤ/Nℤ)^×} |ψ(x;N,m) − x/φ(N)| ≤ c·x(log x)^{−A} for Q = x^{1/2}(log x)^{−B}. Its proof is the SV.3 decomposition still to be done (gap 'SV.3 remaining source decomposition').
The conclusion compares with π(x)/φ(q), as Maynard does, and not with li(x)/φ(q).
proofSteps: Input: Kedlaya Theorem 18.4. Its N=1 term alone gives |ψ(x) − x| ≤ c·x(log x)^{−A}.

Prime powers: in every progression |ψ(t;q,a) − θ(t;q,a)| ≤ |ψ(t) − θ(t)| ≤ 2√t·log t (Mathlib abs_psi_sub_theta_le_sqrt_mul_log). Summed over q≤x^θ this costs O(x^{θ+1/2} log x), which is O(x/(log x)^A) because θ<1/2.

Abel summation with f = 1/log (sum_mul_eq_sub_sub_integral_mul): π(x;q,a) = θ(x;q,a)/log x + ∫_2^x θ(t;q,a)/(t log²t) dt, and the same holds for π(x) with θ(t). Hence |π(x;q,a) − π(x)/φ(q)| ≤ E(x;q)/log x + ∫_2^x E(t;q)/(t log²t) dt + φ(q)^{−1}(|θ(x) − x|/log x + ∫_2^x |θ(t) − t|/(t log²t) dt), where E(t;q) = max_{(a,q)=1} |θ(t;q,a) − t/φ(q)|.

Split the integrals at t₀ = x/(log x)^{A+2}. For t≤t₀ the trivial bound E(t;q) ≤ (t/q + 1 + t/φ(q))·log t suffices. For t₀<t≤x and x large, x^θ ≤ t^{1/2}(log t)^{−B} because θ<1/2, so Theorem 18.4 at t covers every q≤x^θ.
Sum over q≤x^θ using Σ_{q≤y} 1/φ(q) = O(log y). Every term is O(x/(log x)^A).
acceptance: θ<1/2 is strict: the theorem gives no level 1/2 (Maynard, p. 384).
Instance: θ = 1/2 − ε is the input of Maynard Theorem 1.3.
The implied constants are ineffective, through Siegel's theorem inside Theorem 18.4. Maynard's remark after Lemma 5.2 records this.

nodes.title: Selberg's diagonal sum in dimension one (GGPY Lemma 3, κ=1)
nodes.statement: Under (Ω₁) and (Ω₂(1,L)), the partial products of ∏_p (1 − γ(p)/p)^{−1}(1 − 1/p) converge to some c_γ, and for z≥2, Σ_{d<z} μ²(d)g(d) = c_γ log z + O(c_γ L). The implied constant depends only on A₁ and A₂.
hypotheses: γ is multiplicative, A₁>1, A₂≥0 and L≥1. (Ω₁): 0 ≤ γ(p)/p ≤ 1 − 1/A₁ for every prime p. (Ω₂(1,L)): −L ≤ Σ_{w≤p<z} γ(p)log p/p − log(z/w) ≤ A₂ for 2≤w≤z. g(d) = ∏_{p|d} γ(p)/(p − γ(p)) on squarefree d. GGPY state (2.3) as γ(p)/p ≤ 1 − 1/A₁; Maynard's Lemma 6.1 writes 1 − A₁, an equivalent reparametrization.
Only squarefree d contribute, so g need only be defined on squarefree integers. Maynard calls it totally multiplicative.
proofSteps: Outline only: the source proof is Halberstam–Richert, Lemmas 5.3–5.4, which was not read (gap). Write G(y) = Σ_{d<y} μ²(d)g(d). For squarefree d, log d = Σ_{p|d} log p, so Σ_{d<z} μ²(d)g(d) log d = Σ_{p<z} g(p) log p·G_p(z/p), where G_p is G restricted to d coprime to p.
By (Ω₁), G_p(y) = G(y) + O(g(p)G(y)) and Σ_p g(p)² log p = O_{A₁}(1). By (Ω₂) and Abel summation, Σ_{p<z} g(p) log p·G(z/p) = ∫_1^z G(u) du/u + O((L+1)G(z)).

Abel summation on the left-hand side gives G(z) log z − ∫_1^z G(t) dt/t. Hence G(z) log z = 2∫_1^z G(t) dt/t + O((L+1)G(z)). The solution of this integral relation is G(z) = c·log z + O(cL), by the Levin–Fainleib iteration in H–R Lemma 5.3.

Identify c = c_γ. The Dirichlet series Σ μ²(d)g(d)d^{−s} equals ζ(s+1)H(s) with H(s) = ∏_p (1 + g(p)p^{−s})(1 − p^{−1−s}), and H(0) = c_γ. Convergence of the partial products follows from (Ω₂) and Mertens' estimate Σ_{w≤p<z} log p/p = log(z/w) + O(1) (requested from AN.2), by partial summation against 1/log p.
acceptance: γ(p) = 1 for p∤W and γ(p) = 0 for p|W gives g(d) = 1/φ(d) on d coprime to W and c_γ = φ(W)/W, so Σ_{d<z,(d,W)=1} μ²(d)/φ(d) = (φ(W)/W)(log z + O(L)) with L ≪ 1 + Σ_{p|W} log p/p (Maynard (6.7)–(6.8)).
The constant is independent of L and of γ beyond A₁ and A₂. Maynard uses this uniformity with L ≪ log log N.

nodes.title: Smoothly weighted diagonal sum (Maynard Lemma 6.1, GGPY Lemma 4)
nodes.statement: Under (Ω₁) and (Ω₂(1,L)), for G: [0,1]→ℝ of class C¹ with G_max = sup_{[0,1]}(|G| + |G′|): Σ_{d<z} μ²(d)g(d)G(log d/log z) = c_γ log z ∫_0^1 G(x) dx + O(c_γ L G_max). The implied constant depends only on A₁ and A₂, not on L or G.
hypotheses: γ is multiplicative, A₁>1, A₂≥0 and L≥1. (Ω₁): 0 ≤ γ(p)/p ≤ 1 − 1/A₁ for every prime p. (Ω₂(1,L)): −L ≤ Σ_{w≤p<z} γ(p)log p/p − log(z/w) ≤ A₂ for 2≤w≤z. g(d) = ∏_{p|d} γ(p)/(p − γ(p)) on squarefree d. GGPY state (2.3) as γ(p)/p ≤ 1 − 1/A₁; Maynard's Lemma 6.1 writes 1 − A₁, an equivalent reparametrization.
GGPY state Lemma 4 for piecewise differentiable F evaluated at log(z/d)/log z. With G(x) = F(1−x) this is Maynard's form, with ∫_0^1 G = ∫_0^1 F(1−x) dx. Maynard writes S for c_γ.
proofSteps: Write the sum as the Stieltjes integral ∫_{1−}^{z} G(log u/log z) d𝒢(u), where 𝒢(u) = Σ_{d<u} μ²(d)g(d) = c_γ log u + E(u) and |E(u)| ≤ C c_γ L by SV.1/selberg-diagonal-sum-dimension-one.
Main part: the substitution u = z^x gives c_γ log z ∫_0^1 G(x) dx.
The E part: integrate by parts (Abel summation). The boundary terms are at most G_max·C c_γ L, and ∫_1^z |E(u)||G′(log u/log z)| du/(u log z) ≤ C c_γ L G_max.
acceptance: Maynard applies it with γ from (6.7), (6.11) and (6.19), obtaining (6.9), (6.13) and (6.21).
G ≡ 1 recovers SV.1/selberg-diagonal-sum-dimension-one.

nodes.title: Admissible tuple
nodes.statement: A finite set H of nonnegative integers is admissible if, for every prime p, there is an integer a_p with a_p ≢ h (mod p) for every h∈H.
hypotheses: H is a Finset ℕ. The empty set is admissible. Only primes p≤#H can obstruct admissibility, since #H elements meet at most #H residue classes.
proofSteps: Define IsAdmissible H as: for every prime p there is a with ¬ h ≡ a [MOD p] for all h∈H.
Characterisation: H misses a class mod p exactly when the image of reduction mod p has fewer than p elements, which is automatic for p>#H. This makes the predicate decidable.
Monotonicity under subsets and invariance under translation h ↦ h+c (replace a_p by a_p + c) are immediate.
isAdmissible_of_forall_not_dvd: if no element is divisible by a prime p≤#H, residue 0 is missed for those p.
acceptance: {0,2,6,8,12} (Theorem 1.4) and Engelsma's 105-element set (footnote 2) are admissible. {0,2,4} is not, since it covers ℤ/3.

nodes.title: The prime k-tuples conjecture, as a named statement
nodes.statement: For a finite H⊂ℕ let primeTranslates(H) = {n : n+h is prime for every h∈H}. The prime k-tuples conjecture asserts that primeTranslates(H) is infinite for every admissible H.
hypotheses: It is a named statement, not an assumption. RS-07 moves the prime-tuple statement register here from AnalyticNumberTheory:AN.6, separately from Maynard's proven theorems.
proofSteps: Define primeTranslates and PrimeTuplesConjecture as displayed.
Necessity: if H covers every class mod p, then for each n some n+h is divisible by p, hence equals p. So n ≤ p, and primeTranslates(H) is finite.
The singleton {0} gives the set of primes (Mathlib infinite_setOfPred_prime), and {0,2} gives the twin primes.
acceptance: Maynard's proven statement (SV.4/positive-proportion-prime-tuples) is a positive-proportion result, not this conjecture. The twin prime conjecture is the case H = {0,2}, and it is not proved.

nodes.title: The W-trick residue v₀ (Maynard (4.1))
nodes.statement: For real D₀ let W = ∏_{p≤D₀} p, the primorial of ⌊D₀⌋. For admissible H there is v₀ with 0≤v₀<W and gcd(v₀+h, W) = 1 for every h∈H; wResidue(H,D₀) is the least such v₀ (0 if none exists). Maynard takes D₀ = log log log N, and then W ≪ (log log N)².
hypotheses: H is admissible. Only ⌊D₀⌋ matters.
AdditiveCombinatorics:AC.4 plans a separate W-trick for the Green–Tao majorant (one linear form). RS-07 keeps the two apart; this is the tuple version.
proofSteps: For each prime p≤D₀, admissibility gives a class a_p missed by H. Require v₀ ≡ −a_p (mod p); then v₀+h ≡ h − a_p ≢ 0 (mod p) for every h∈H.
The primes p≤D₀ are pairwise coprime, so Nat.chineseRemainderOfFinset gives v₀ mod W. Minimality: take Nat.find of the decidable existence statement over v<W.
W ≤ 4^{⌊D₀⌋} ≤ 4^{D₀} by primorial_le_four_pow. With D₀ = log log log N, 4^{D₀} = (log log N)^{log 4} ≤ (log log N)² for large N.
acceptance: For H = {0,2} and D₀ = 3: W = 6 and v₀ = 5, since 5 and 7 are both coprime to 6.

nodes.title: Maynard's multidimensional sieve weights
nodes.statement: Fix k, W, R>1 and F: ℝ^k→ℝ. For r∈ℕ^k put y_r = F(log r₁/log R, …, log r_k/log R) when ∏rᵢ is squarefree, coprime to W and less than R, and y_r = 0 otherwise (6.3). Define λ_d = (∏ μ(dᵢ)dᵢ) Σ_{r: dᵢ|rᵢ} y_r/∏φ(rᵢ) (5.8), and the weight w_n = (Σ_{dᵢ|n+hᵢ ∀i} λ_d)² (2.4). With these, S₁ = Σ_{N≤n<2N, n≡v₀ (W)} w_n, S₂^{(m)} = Σ_{same n} χ_P(n+h_m)w_n, and y^{(m)}_r = (∏ μ(rᵢ)g(rᵢ)) Σ_{rᵢ|dᵢ, d_m=1} λ_d/∏φ(dᵢ), where g is totally multiplicative with g(p) = p−2 ((4.2), (5.14), (5.23)).
hypotheses: λ built from a general y (maynardLambdaOfY) is what Lemmas 5.1–5.3 use; maynardLambda specializes to (6.3). Proposition 4.1 writes λ directly from F and replaces ∏rᵢ<R by 'F supported on ℛ_k'. The two differ only at ∏rᵢ = R, which does not affect the asymptotics.
All sums are finite: rᵢ and dᵢ run below ⌈R⌉, and every other term vanishes by the support condition.
proofSteps: Define y, λ, w, S₁, S₂^{(m)}, g and y^{(m)} as displayed.
Support: if dᵢ|rᵢ for all i, then ∏dᵢ divides ∏rᵢ. So some y_r in the sum can be nonzero only if ∏dᵢ is squarefree, coprime to W and less than R.
Inversion (5.7)–(5.8): substitute the definition and use Σ_{dᵢ|rᵢ|eᵢ} μ(rᵢ) = μ(dᵢ)·[eᵢ = dᵢ] for squarefree eᵢ.
Dimension one: (Σ_{d|m} λ_d)² = Σ_{e|m} Σ_{lcm(d₁,d₂)=e} λ_{d₁}λ_{d₂} = Σ_{e|m} lambdaSquared(λ)(e).
acceptance: For R = 2 only r = (1,…,1) is supported, so λ_{(1,…,1)} = F(0), every other λ_d vanishes, and w_n = F(0)² for every n.
The weights depend on (d₁,…,d_k) jointly, not only on ∏dᵢ. This is the new feature of the method (p. 387).

nodes.title: Maynard's variational quantity M_k
nodes.statement: Let ℛ_k = {t∈[0,1]^k : Σtᵢ ≤ 1}. For F: [0,1]^k→ℝ put I_k(F) = ∫F² and J_k^{(m)}(F) = ∫(∫_0^1 F dt_m)² dt₁…dt_{m−1}dt_{m+1}…dt_k. Let 𝒮_k be the set of F supported on ℛ_k with I_k(F) ≠ 0 and J_k^{(m)}(F) ≠ 0 for every m. Then M_k = sup_{F∈𝒮_k} Σ_m J_k^{(m)}(F)/I_k(F).
hypotheses: Maynard's 𝒮_k consists of Riemann-integrable functions; here it consists of square-integrable functions on the cube. The suprema agree: every Riemann-integrable function is square-integrable, and SV.4/ratio-smooth-approximation approximates every square-integrable member by smooth functions supported on ℛ_k.
J^{(m)} is integrated over the whole cube. Its integrand does not depend on t_m, so this is the (k−1)-fold integral of the source.
G_{b,j} of Lemma 8.1 is included as data, with the r = 0 term (E31).
proofSteps: Define ℛ_k, I_k, J_k^{(m)}, the admissible class, the ratio, and M_k as the supremum of a set of reals bounded above by k.
Upper bound: by Cauchy–Schwarz, (∫_0^1 F dt_m)² ≤ ∫_0^1 F² dt_m. So J^{(m)} ≤ I and M_k ≤ k.
Replacing F by cF multiplies I and each J^{(m)} by c². Permuting the coordinates permutes the J^{(m)}.
Radial case F = G(Σtᵢ) on ℛ_k: slice by s = Σ_{i≠m} tᵢ, whose density on ℛ_{k−1} is s^{k−2}/(k−2)!. This gives the GPY integrals of the remark after Lemma 6.3.
acceptance: M₁ = 1: J^{(1)} = (∫F)² ≤ ∫F², with equality for F = 1 on [0,1].
The support condition is essential: F ≡ 1 on the cube has ratio k.

nodes.title: Smooth approximation within the simplex
nodes.statement: For F∈𝒮_k and δ>0 there is a smooth F₁∈𝒮_k, supported on ℛ_k, with I_k(F₁) > 0 and ratio(F₁) > ratio(F) − δ. In particular M_k is also the supremum over smooth functions supported on ℛ_k.
hypotheses: 𝒮_k is the L² class of SV.4/maynard-functionals.
proofSteps: Shrink: F_η(t) = F((t − η𝟙)/(1 − (k+1)η)) vanishes unless tᵢ ≥ η and Σtᵢ ≤ 1 − η. I scales by (1 − (k+1)η)^k and each J^{(m)} by (1 − (k+1)η)^{k+1}, so the ratio is multiplied by 1 − (k+1)η.
Mollify: convolve F_η with a smooth bump (Mathlib ContDiffBump) of radius below η/√k. The result is smooth, supported in ℛ_k, and converges to F_η in L²(cube) as the radius tends to 0.

Continuity: F ↦ ∫_0^1 F dt_m is 1-Lipschitz from L²(cube) to L²(cube) by Cauchy–Schwarz, so I and each J^{(m)} are continuous. For η and the radius small enough, the ratio moves by less than δ and I and the J^{(m)} stay nonzero.
acceptance: Maynard's proof of Proposition 4.2 uses this step without proof; it is supplied here.

sources.match: The approximation step. The proof is worker-derived.

nodes.title: The GPY positivity criterion
nodes.statement: Let H be finite, N∈ℕ, w_n ≥ 0 and ρ∈ℝ. If Σ_{N≤n<2N} (#{h∈H : n+h prime} − ρ)w_n > 0, then some n∈[N,2N) has more than ρ, hence at least ⌊ρ+1⌋, of the n+h prime.
hypotheses: No arithmetic input. The weights need only be nonnegative.
proofSteps: If every n had at most ρ of the n+h prime, each summand (#{…} − ρ)w_n would be ≤ 0, because w_n ≥ 0, and so would the sum.
An integer c > ρ satisfies c ≥ ⌊ρ⌋ + 1 = ⌊ρ + 1⌋.
acceptance: With ρ = θM_k/2 − ε this is the positivity step of Proposition 4.2. For small ε>0, ⌊ρ+1⌋ = ⌈θM_k/2⌉.

sources.match: The criterion.

nodes.title: Size of λ in terms of y (Maynard (5.9))
nodes.statement: If y vanishes off the support (∏rᵢ squarefree, coprime to W, less than R) and |y_r| ≤ y_max, then |λ_d| ≤ y_max Σ_{u<R} μ²(u)τ_k(u)/φ(u) for every d. The right-hand side is O_k(y_max (log R)^k).
hypotheses: τ_k(u) is the number of ordered factorizations u = c₁⋯c_k.
proofSteps: Insert |y_r| ≤ y_max into (5.8) and write rᵢ = dᵢr′ᵢ. Since ∏rᵢ is squarefree, the r′ᵢ are coprime to ∏dᵢ.
Use d/φ(d) = Σ_{e|d} 1/φ(e) for squarefree d and the multiplicativity of φ to combine everything into Σ_{u<R} μ²(u)τ_k(u)/φ(u), with u = dr′ and τ_k(dr′) ≥ τ_k(r′) (5.9).

Σ_{u<R} μ²(u)τ_k(u)/φ(u) ≤ ∏_{p<R}(1 + k/(p−1)) ≤ exp(k Σ_{p<R} 1/(p−1)) = O_k((log R)^k). This uses Σ_{p<R} 1/p = log log R + O(1), which follows from Mertens' first theorem (requested from AN.2) by partial summation.
acceptance: The O_k((log R)^k) bound is what turns the error O(λ_max²R²(log R)^{2k}) of (5.3) into O(y_max²R²(log R)^{4k}).

sources.match: The bound. The final Mertens estimate is made explicit here.

nodes.title: Diagonal form of S₁ (Maynard Lemma 5.1)
nodes.statement: Let y vanish off the support, with |y_r| ≤ y_max, and λ = λ(y). Then S₁ = (N/W) Σ_r y_r²/∏φ(rᵢ) + O(y_max² φ(W)^k N(log R)^k/(W^{k+1}D₀)).
hypotheses: N is large, D₀ = log log log N, W = ∏_{p≤D₀}p, v₀ is the W-trick residue of the admissible H = {h₁,…,h_k} (distinct), R = N^{θ/2−δ} with 0<θ≤1 and δ>0 fixed. The implied constants depend on k, H, θ and δ, and not on N, y or F.
proofSteps: Expand the square and swap the sums (5.1). By the Chinese remainder theorem, the count of N≤n<2N with n≡v₀ (W) and [dᵢ,eᵢ] | n+hᵢ is N/q + O(1), q = W∏[dᵢ,eᵢ], when W, [d₁,e₁], …, [d_k,e_k] are pairwise coprime. Otherwise it is 0: a prime dividing [dᵢ,eᵢ] and [dⱼ,eⱼ] divides hᵢ − hⱼ and exceeds D₀ > max|hᵢ − hⱼ| (5.2).
The O(1) terms: λ is supported on ∏dᵢ < R, so they total ≪ λ_max²(Σ_{d<R} τ_k(d))² ≪ λ_max²R²(log R)^{2k} (5.3), with λ_max ≪ y_max(log R)^k (SV.4/lambda-max-bound).
Main term: 1/[dᵢ,eᵢ] = (dᵢeᵢ)^{−1} Σ_{uᵢ|dᵢ,eᵢ} φ(uᵢ) (5.4). Remove the remaining conditions (dᵢ,eⱼ) = 1 (i≠j) with Möbius sums over s_{i,j}, restricted as in the source (5.5)–(5.6).

Substitute the change of variables (5.7)–(5.8) to get (5.11). Every s_{i,j} ≠ 1 is coprime to W, hence exceeds D₀; these terms contribute O(y_max²φ(W)^kN(log R)^k/(W^{k+1}D₀)) (5.12), using Σ_{u<R,(u,W)=1} μ²(u)/φ(u) ≪ (φ(W)/W) log R (SV.1/selberg-diagonal-sum-dimension-one).
R² ≤ N^{1−2δ} and W ≪ N^δ, so the O(y_max²R²(log R)^{4k}) error is smaller than the first (5.13).
acceptance: The main term is diagonal in y: the change of variables diagonalizes the quadratic form S₁, as in the main term of Selberg's one-dimensional sieve (compare Mathlib's lambdaSquared).

sources.match: The lemma and the steps of its proof.

nodes.title: Diagonal form of S₂^{(m)} (Maynard Lemma 5.2)
nodes.statement: Assume in addition that the primes have level of distribution θ, that k ≥ 2, and fix A>0. Then S₂^{(m)} = N/(φ(W) log N) Σ_r (y^{(m)}_r)²/∏g(rᵢ) + O((y^{(m)}_max)² φ(W)^{k−2}N(log N)^{k−2}/(W^{k−1}D₀)) + O(y_max² N/(log N)^A).
hypotheses: N is large, D₀ = log log log N, W = ∏_{p≤D₀}p, v₀ is the W-trick residue of the admissible H = {h₁,…,h_k} (distinct), R = N^{θ/2−δ} with 0<θ≤1 and δ>0 fixed. The implied constants depend on k, H, θ and δ, and not on N, y or F.
y^{(m)}_max bounds |y^{(m)}_r| for every r.
proofSteps: Expand as for S₁ (5.15). The inner sum runs over one class mod q = W∏[dᵢ,eᵢ] and is coprime to q exactly when d_m = e_m = 1. It equals X_N/φ(q) + O(E(N,q)), where X_N = #{N≤n<2N : n prime} and E is windowError (5.16)–(5.18).

Error: q is squarefree and less than R²W, and each q arises from at most τ_{3k}(q) tuples. With λ_max ≪ y_max(log R)^k the error is ≪ y_max²(log R)^{2k} Σ_{q<R²W} μ²(q)τ_{3k}(q)E(N,q). Cauchy–Schwarz with E(N,q) ≪ N/φ(q) and PrimesHaveLevel.sum_windowError (R²W < N^{θ−δ} for large N) give ≪ y_max²N/(log N)^A (5.19)–(5.20).

Main term: write 1/φ([dᵢ,eᵢ]) = (φ(dᵢ)φ(eᵢ))^{−1} Σ_{uᵢ|dᵢ,eᵢ} g(uᵢ) (5.21), remove the cross coprimality with Möbius sums, and substitute y^{(m)} (5.23) to get (5.24). Terms with s_{i,j} ≠ 1 contribute the D₀ error (5.25).
Replace X_N by N/log N + O(N/(log N)²), by the prime number theorem (requested from AN.2); the error is absorbed (5.26)–(5.27).
acceptance: This is the only use of the arithmetic hypothesis. Unconditional results come from SV.3/bombieri-vinogradov-level.
The implied constants are ineffective through Bombieri–Vinogradov (remark after Lemma 5.2).

sources.match: The lemma and the steps of its proof.

nodes.title: y^{(m)} in terms of y (Maynard Lemma 5.3)
nodes.statement: If r_m = 1, then y^{(m)}_r = Σ_{a_m} y_{r₁,…,r_{m−1},a_m,r_{m+1},…,r_k}/φ(a_m) + O(y_max φ(W) log R/(W D₀)).
hypotheses: N is large, D₀ = log log log N, W = ∏_{p≤D₀}p, v₀ is the W-trick residue of the admissible H = {h₁,…,h_k} (distinct), R = N^{θ/2−δ} with 0<θ≤1 and δ>0 fixed. The implied constants depend on k, H, θ and δ, and not on N, y or F.
proofSteps: Substitute (5.8) into (5.23) (5.28), then swap the d and a sums (5.29).
Evaluate Σ_{rᵢ|dᵢ|aᵢ} μ(dᵢ)dᵢ/φ(dᵢ) = μ(aᵢ)rᵢ/φ(aᵢ) for squarefree aᵢ (5.30).
Since (aⱼ,W) = 1, either aⱼ = rⱼ or aⱼ > D₀rⱼ. The terms with aⱼ > D₀rⱼ contribute O(y_max φ(W) log R/(WD₀)), using Σ_{a_m<R,(a_m,W)=1} μ²(a_m)/φ(a_m) ≪ (φ(W)/W) log R (5.31).
When aⱼ = rⱼ for every j≠m, the factor ∏g(rᵢ)rᵢ/φ(rᵢ)² is 1 + O(1/D₀), because g(p)p/φ(p)² = 1 − 1/(p−1)² and every prime factor exceeds D₀ (5.32).
acceptance: y^{(m)} vanishes unless r_m = 1; the lemma is the only link between y^{(m)} and y.

sources.match: The lemma and the steps of its proof.

nodes.title: Asymptotic for S₁ (Maynard Lemma 6.2)
nodes.statement: S₁ = φ(W)^k N(log R)^k I_k(F)/W^{k+1} + O(F_max² φ(W)^k N(log R)^k/(W^{k+1}D₀)).
hypotheses: N is large, D₀ = log log log N, W = ∏_{p≤D₀}p, v₀ is the W-trick residue of the admissible H = {h₁,…,h_k} (distinct), R = N^{θ/2−δ} with 0<θ≤1 and δ>0 fixed. The implied constants depend on k, H, θ and δ, and not on N, y or F.
F is of class C¹ and supported on ℛ_k, and F_max = sup_{[0,1]^k} (|F| + Σᵢ|∂F/∂tᵢ|); y = y(F) is given by (6.3).
proofSteps: Insert (6.3) into Lemma 5.1 (6.4); y_max ≤ F_max.
Drop the pairwise coprimality of the uᵢ: two integers coprime to W with a common factor share a prime greater than D₀. This costs O(F_max²φ(W)^kN(log R)^k/(W^{k+1}D₀)) (6.5).
Apply SV.1/selberg-smooth-diagonal-sum k times, once in each variable, with γ(p) = 1 for p∤W and γ(p) = 0 for p|W. Then c_γ = φ(W)/W and L ≪ 1 + Σ_{p|W} log p/p ≪ log D₀ by Mertens (6.7)–(6.9).
Combine: the error O(log D₀ (log R)^{k−1}) is smaller than (log R)^k/D₀.
acceptance: The main term is positive whenever I_k(F) ≠ 0.

sources.match: The lemma and the steps of its proof.

nodes.title: Asymptotic for S₂^{(m)} (Maynard Lemma 6.3)
nodes.statement: If the primes have level of distribution θ, then S₂^{(m)} = φ(W)^k N(log R)^{k+1} J_k^{(m)}(F)/(W^{k+1} log N) + O(F_max² φ(W)^k N(log R)^k/(W^{k+1}D₀)).
hypotheses: N is large, D₀ = log log log N, W = ∏_{p≤D₀}p, v₀ is the W-trick residue of the admissible H = {h₁,…,h_k} (distinct), R = N^{θ/2−δ} with 0<θ≤1 and δ>0 fixed. The implied constants depend on k, H, θ and δ, and not on N, y or F.
F is of class C¹ and supported on ℛ_k, and F_max = sup_{[0,1]^k} (|F| + Σᵢ|∂F/∂tᵢ|); y = y(F) is given by (6.3).
proofSteps: By Lemma 5.3 and (6.3): if r_m = 1 and ∏rᵢ is squarefree and coprime to W, then y^{(m)}_r = Σ_{(u,W∏rᵢ)=1} μ²(u)/φ(u)·F(…, log u/log R, …) + O(F_max φ(W) log R/(WD₀)) (6.10). In particular y^{(m)}_max ≪ φ(W)F_max log R/W.

Apply SV.1/selberg-smooth-diagonal-sum in u with γ(p) = 1 for p∤W∏rᵢ, where L ≪ log log N (6.11)–(6.12). This gives y^{(m)}_r = (log R)(φ(W)/W)∏(φ(rᵢ)/rᵢ)·F^{(m)}_r + O(…), where F^{(m)}_r = ∫_0^1 F(…, t_m, …) dt_m (6.13)–(6.14).
Substitute into Lemma 5.2 (6.15)–(6.16) and drop the coprimality of the rᵢ at the cost (6.17).
Apply SV.1/selberg-smooth-diagonal-sum to each rᵢ (i≠m) with γ(p) = 1 − (p²−3p+1)/(p³−p²−2p+1) for p∤W, for which γ(p)/(p−γ(p)) = φ(p)²/(g(p)p²) (6.19). The result is J_k^{(m)} (6.21)–(6.22).
acceptance: Check of (6.19): p(p−1)²/(p³−p²−2p+1) = 1 − (p²−3p+1)/(p³−p²−2p+1). arXiv v2 printed a different γ; v3 and the published text agree on this one.

sources.match: The lemma and the steps of its proof.

nodes.title: Maynard's asymptotics for S₁ and S₂ (Proposition 4.1)
nodes.statement: Let the primes have level of distribution θ∈(0,1], let R = N^{θ/2−δ} with δ>0 fixed, and let F be smooth and supported on ℛ_k with I_k(F) ≠ 0 and J_k^{(m)}(F) ≠ 0 for every m. With λ built from F: S₁ = (1+o(1)) φ(W)^k N(log R)^k I_k(F)/W^{k+1}, and for every m, S₂^{(m)} = (1+o(1)) φ(W)^k N(log R)^{k+1} J_k^{(m)}(F)/(W^{k+1} log N); hence S₂ = Σ_m S₂^{(m)} has the stated asymptotic.
hypotheses: N is large, D₀ = log log log N, W = ∏_{p≤D₀}p, v₀ is the W-trick residue of the admissible H = {h₁,…,h_k} (distinct), R = N^{θ/2−δ} with 0<θ≤1 and δ>0 fixed. The implied constants depend on k, H, θ and δ, and not on N, y or F.
Maynard states Proposition 4.1 with 'exponent of distribution θ'; it is the level of distribution of (1.3).
proofSteps: Apply Lemmas 6.2 and 6.3 with F fixed: F_max is a constant and D₀ → ∞, so each error term is o(main term), because I_k(F) and J_k^{(m)}(F) are nonzero.
The λ of Proposition 4.1 is the construction from (6.3), by the inversion (5.8).
acceptance: The S₂ asymptotic, summed over m, is Proposition 4.1's display with Σ_m J_k^{(m)}(F).

sources.match: The proposition. Its proof is §§5–6, decomposed in the lemmas above.

nodes.title: Primes in admissible tuples (Maynard Proposition 4.2)
nodes.statement: Let the primes have level of distribution θ∈(0,1] and let H = {h₁,…,h_k} be admissible. With r_k = ⌈θM_k/2⌉, there are infinitely many n such that at least r_k of n+h₁, …, n+h_k are prime. In particular liminf_n (p_{n+r_k−1} − p_n) ≤ max_{i,j}(hᵢ − hⱼ).
hypotheses: The hᵢ are distinct. M_k is the quantity of SV.4/maynard-functionals.
proofSteps: Choose F₀∈𝒮_k with ratio > M_k − δ, and then a smooth F₁ with ratio > M_k − 2δ (SV.4/ratio-smooth-approximation).

Proposition 4.1 for F₁ gives S = S₂ − ρS₁ = (φ(W)^kN(log R)^k I_k(F₁)/W^{k+1})·((log R/log N) Σ_m J^{(m)}(F₁) − ρI(F₁) + o(1)) ≥ (…)·((θ/2 − δ)(M_k − 2δ) − ρ + o(1)). This is (4.4), whose printed sum index j should be m (E27).

Take ρ = θM_k/2 − ε, with δ small in terms of ε. Then S > 0 for all large N. The weights are nonnegative, so the positivity criterion gives, for each large N, some n∈[N,2N) with at least ⌊ρ+1⌋ = ⌈θM_k/2⌉ of the n+hᵢ prime (ε small).
Since this holds for every large N, there are infinitely many such n. The gap statement is SV.4/clustered-primes-to-gaps.
acceptance: k = 105 and θ = 1/2 − ε give r₁₀₅ ≥ 2 (Theorem 1.3). k = 5 and θ = 1 − ε give r₅ ≥ 2 under Elliott–Halberstam (Theorem 1.4).

sources.match: The proposition and its proof.

planet.name: Maynard's refinement of the GPY sieve

nodes.title: From prime clusters to prime gaps
nodes.statement: Let H be finite and nonempty and r ≥ 1. If infinitely many n have at least r of the n+h (h∈H) prime, then p_{j+r−1} − p_j ≤ max H − min H for infinitely many j, i.e. liminf_j (p_{j+r−1} − p_j) ≤ max H − min H. Here p_j is the j-th prime, counted from 0.
hypotheses: Maynard's p_n is 1-indexed. Differences p_{n+m} − p_n are unaffected by the shift.
proofSteps: For such an n, let q₁ < … < q_r be r of the primes among the n+h, and let j be the index of q₁. The r primes lie in [q₁, q_r], so p_{j+r−1} ≤ q_r and p_{j+r−1} − p_j ≤ q_r − q₁ ≤ max H − min H.
Distinct large n give arbitrarily large q₁, hence infinitely many j.
acceptance: With r = 2 and H of diameter 600 this is the step from Proposition 4.2 to liminf(p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 600.

sources.match: The deduction, which the source leaves implicit.

nodes.title: Lower bound for M_k when k is large (Maynard Proposition 4.3(3))
nodes.statement: For all sufficiently large k, M_k > log k − 2 log log k − 2.
hypotheses: The implied constants in §7 are independent of k.
proofSteps: Take F(t) = ∏g(ktᵢ) on ℛ_k (7.3), with g supported on [0,T], γ = ∫g², and μ = ∫ug²/γ < 1 − T/k (7.8). Then I_k ≤ k^{−k}γ^k (7.4), and J_k ≥ J′_k − E_k with J′_k = k^{−k−1}γ^{k−1}(∫g)² (7.5)–(7.7).

Bound E_k by a second moment. With η = (k−T)/(k−1) − μ > 0, 1 ≤ η^{−2}(Σ_{i≥2}uᵢ/(k−1) − μ)² on the error region (7.9). Drop the constraint Σ_{i=2}^k uᵢ > k−T (printed with i=1, E30) and expand the square: E_k ≤ η^{−2}μTk^{−k−1}γ^{k−1}(∫g)²/(k−1) (7.10)–(7.13).
Hence kJ_k/I_k ≥ ((∫g)²/∫g²)·(1 − T/(k(1 − T/k − μ)²)) (7.14). This uses (k−1)η² ≥ k(1 − T/k − μ)², which holds because η = x + (k−T)/(k(k−1)) with x = 1 − T/k − μ and 2(k−T)/k ≥ x.
Choose g(t) = 1/(1+At) on [0,T] with 1 + AT = e^A (7.16)–(7.18), and A = log k − 2 log log k (7.20)–(7.21).
acceptance: Only the leading term log k matters for Theorem 1.1. The −2 absorbs the loss log k/((log k)² + O(1)) in (7.21).

sources.match: The construction and estimates.

nodes.title: Moments on the simplex (Maynard Lemma 8.1, corrected)
nodes.statement: For integers k ≥ 1 and a, b, j ≥ 0: ∫_{ℛ_k} (1 − P₁)^a P_j^b dt = (a! b!/(k+a+jb)!) Σ_{b₁+…+b_k=b} ∏ᵢ (jbᵢ)!/bᵢ! = (a!/(k+jb+a)!)·G_{b,j}(k). Here P_j = Σtᵢ^j and G_{b,j}(x) = b! Σ_{r=0}^{b} C(x,r) Σ_{b₁,…,b_r≥1, Σbᵢ=b} ∏(jbᵢ)!/bᵢ!. The term r = 0, which makes G_{0,j} = 1, is needed; the printed formula starts at r = 1 (E31).
hypotheses: The multinomial form, summed over all (b₁,…,b_k) including zero entries, needs no convention at b = 0.
proofSteps: Dirichlet integral (8.2): ∫_{ℛ_k}(1−Σtᵢ)^a ∏tᵢ^{aᵢ} = a!∏aᵢ!/(k + a + Σaᵢ)!. Prove it by induction on k: integrate t₁ over [0, 1 − Σ_{i≥2}tᵢ] with v = t₁/(1 − Σ_{i≥2}tᵢ) and use the Beta integral ∫_0^1 t^a(1−t)^b dt = a!b!/(a+b+1)! (from Mathlib's Γ–Beta identity) (8.3).
Expand P_j^b by the multinomial theorem (8.4) and apply (8.2); this gives (8.5).
Group the tuples by the number r of nonzero bᵢ (8.6). For b = 0 the only tuple is zero, which is the r = 0 term.
acceptance: k = 5, a = 2, b = 0: the integral is 2!/7! = 1/2520, while the printed formula gives 0.

sources.match: The lemma, corrected at b = 0.

nodes.title: I_k and J_k as quadratic forms (Maynard Lemma 8.2)
nodes.statement: For P = Σ_{i=1}^d aᵢ(1 − P₁)^{bᵢ}P₂^{cᵢ} and F = P on ℛ_k (0 elsewhere), with k ≥ 2: I_k(F) = Σ_{i,j} aᵢaⱼ(bᵢ+bⱼ)! G_{cᵢ+cⱼ,2}(k)/(k+bᵢ+bⱼ+2cᵢ+2cⱼ)!, and J_k^{(m)}(F) = Σ_{i,j} aᵢaⱼ Σ_{c′₁≤cᵢ, c′₂≤cⱼ} C(cᵢ,c′₁)C(cⱼ,c′₂)·γ·G_{c′₁+c′₂,2}(k−1)/(k+bᵢ+bⱼ+2cᵢ+2cⱼ+1)!. Here γ = bᵢ!bⱼ!(2cᵢ−2c′₁)!(2cⱼ−2c′₂)!(bᵢ+bⱼ+2cᵢ+2cⱼ−2c′₁−2c′₂+2)!/((bᵢ+2cᵢ−2c′₁+1)!(bⱼ+2cⱼ−2c′₂+1)!), and G includes the r = 0 term (E31). So I_k and Σ_m J_k^{(m)} are quadratic forms aᵀA₁a and aᵀA₂a with rational A₁, A₂.
hypotheses: F is symmetric, so J_k^{(m)} does not depend on m and Σ_m J_k^{(m)} = kJ_k^{(1)}.
proofSteps: I_k: expand P² and apply the corrected Lemma 8.1 with j = 2 (8.7).
J: expand P₂^c = Σ C(c,c′)(P′₂)^{c′} t₁^{2c−2c′} and integrate in t₁ with the Beta integral (8.8); then square (8.9).

Apply Lemma 8.1 on ℛ_{k−1}: ∫_{ℛ_{k−1}}(1−P′₁)^B(P′₂)^{c′} = B! G_{c′,2}(k−1)/(k−1+B+2c′)!. The printed (8.10) has (k+b+c−1)! and G_{c,2} (E32). With B = bᵢ+bⱼ+2cᵢ+2cⱼ−2c′₁−2c′₂+2 the denominator is (k+bᵢ+bⱼ+2cᵢ+2cⱼ+1)!, as in the lemma.
acceptance: k = 5 with (8.16): exact rational arithmetic with these formulas gives I₅ = 29509/1222452000 and ratio 1417255/708216, which agrees with direct integration. The printed G (r ≥ 1) gives I₅ = 17753/977961600 and ratio 26784/17753 ≈ 1.509.
By Lemma 8.3 the best ratio in the span is the largest eigenvalue of A₁^{−1}A₂. A lower bound for M_k needs only one explicit coefficient vector.

nodes.title: Engelsma's admissible 105-tuple of diameter 600
nodes.statement: The 105-element set H₁₀₅ = {0, 10, 12, 24, 28, …, 594, 598, 600} of Maynard's footnote 2 is admissible, contains 0 and 600, and lies in [0,600].

proofSteps: By isAdmissible_iff_card_image_lt, only the 27 primes p ≤ 103 need checking. For each, exhibit a missed residue: for example 1 mod 2, 2 mod 3, 1 mod 5, 4 mod 7, 7 mod 11 and 6 mod 13.
This is a finite, decidable computation.

nodes.title: The first k primes above k are admissible
nodes.statement: For every k, the first k primes greater than k form an admissible set. Its diameter p_{π(k)+k} − p_{π(k)+1} is O(k log k).
hypotheses: In 0-indexed form the set is {nth prime (π(k) + i) : i < k}.
proofSteps: Every element is a prime greater than k, so none is divisible by a prime p ≤ k = #H; apply isAdmissible_of_forall_not_dvd. The published argument says 'less than k', and so omits p = k when k is prime (E29).
Diameter: π(k) + k ≤ 2k, and Chebyshev's lower bound π(x) ≥ c·x/log x (Mathlib pi_ge') gives p_n ≪ n log n.
acceptance: k = 5: {7, 11, 13, 17, 19}. It misses 0 mod 5 because no element is divisible by 5; this is the case p = k.

sources.match: The set and its diameter. The admissibility argument is corrected at p = k.

nodes.title: Bounded gaps between primes (Maynard Theorem 1.3)
nodes.statement: liminf_n (p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 600.
hypotheses: Unconditional. It uses Bombieri–Vinogradov and none of Zhang's technology.
proofSteps: Bombieri–Vinogradov gives level θ = 1/2 − ε. Since M₁₀₅ > 4, θM₁₀₅/2 > 1 for small ε, so r₁₀₅ = ⌈θM₁₀₅/2⌉ ≥ 2.
Proposition 4.2 with Engelsma's admissible H₁₀₅ (diameter 600): infinitely many n have two primes among the n + H₁₀₅. Hence liminf(p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 600.
acceptance: This is not the twin prime conjecture, and 600 is not optimal (Maynard, p. 385).

sources.match: The theorem and its deduction.

nodes.title: Gaps under Elliott–Halberstam (Maynard Theorem 1.4)
nodes.statement: If the primes have level of distribution θ for every θ < 1 (the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture), then liminf(p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 12 and liminf(p_{n+2} − p_n) ≤ 600.
hypotheses: Conditional on the named hypothesis ElliottHalberstam of SV.3/level-of-distribution.
proofSteps: k = 105 and θ = 1 − ε: θM₁₀₅/2 > 2, so three primes occur among n + H₁₀₅ infinitely often, and liminf(p_{n+2} − p_n) ≤ 600.
k = 5, H = {0,2,6,8,12} (admissible, diameter 12) and θ = 1 − ε: θM₅/2 > 1, so liminf(p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 12.
acceptance: 12 appears to be optimal for the method in its current form (Maynard, p. 385).

sources.match: The theorem and its deduction.

nodes.title: m + 1 primes in bounded intervals (Maynard Theorem 1.1)
nodes.statement: There is an absolute constant C such that liminf_n (p_{n+m} − p_n) ≤ C m³ e^{4m} for every m ≥ 1.
hypotheses: Unconditional.
proofSteps: Take θ = 1/2 − 1/k (Bombieri–Vinogradov). By Proposition 4.3(3), θM_k/2 ≥ (1/4 − 1/(2k))(log k − 2 log log k − 2) (4.5), which exceeds m once k ≥ C₀m²e^{4m} for an absolute C₀.
Take k = ⌈C₀m²e^{4m}⌉ and H the first k primes above k, which is admissible with diameter ≪ k log k.
Proposition 4.2 gives m + 1 primes among n + H infinitely often, so liminf(p_{n+m} − p_n) ≪ k log k ≪ m³e^{4m}.
acceptance: Under Elliott–Halberstam the bound improves to O(m³e^{2m}) (Maynard, p. 385); that is not planned here.

sources.match: The theorem and its deduction.

nodes.title: A positive proportion of admissible m-tuples are prime (Maynard Theorem 1.2)
nodes.statement: For every m ≥ 1 there are r₀ and c > 0 such that every set A of r ≥ r₀ distinct nonnegative integers has at least c·C(r,m) subsets {h₁,…,h_m} ⊆ A for which infinitely many n make every n + hᵢ prime.
hypotheses: The source allows arbitrary integers. Translating A by a constant changes neither count, so natural numbers suffice.
proofSteps: With k = ⌈Cm²e^{4m}⌉ as in Theorem 1.1, every admissible k-set contains an m-subset with infinitely many prime translates.
Thin A: for each prime p ≤ k, delete the residue class mod p with the fewest elements. The remainder A₂ has s ≥ r∏_{p≤k}(1 − 1/p) elements, and every k-subset of it is admissible.

Double count: each of the C(s,k) k-subsets contains a good m-subset, and each m-subset lies in C(s−m,k−m) of them. So there are at least C(s,k)/C(s−m,k−m) ≫_m s^m ≫_m r^m good m-subsets, while C(r,m) ≤ r^m.
acceptance: This is a positive-proportion statement, not the prime m-tuples conjecture for any given tuple.

sources.match: The theorem and its deduction.

nodes.title: Logarithmic sieve dimension
nodes.statement: HasLogSieveDimension(P,g,κ,C) means: for every real z≥2, Σ_{p∈P, p prime, p≤z} g(p) log p ≤ κ log z+C. The sum is finite. P is a fixed set of naturals and g is a fixed real function; constants do not depend on z or on an application population.
hypotheses: The predicate records only the displayed inequality. Positivity of g, κ and C are separate theorem hypotheses; it does not assert a local density or any distribution estimate. In Chapter 11 g(p)=ω(p)/p.
proofSteps: Use the finite prime set obtained by filtering naturals up to floor z. Quantify the bound over every real z≥2, not merely a single cutoff.
acceptance: A finite set at a single cutoff does not supply constants uniform across a varying prime family.

sources.match: A quantified version of the source logarithmic condition; explicit C replaces its bounded additive term.

nodes.title: Euler-product sieve dimension
nodes.statement: HasProductSieveDimension(P,g,κ,K) means: for every real 2≤w≤z, ∏_{p∈P, p prime, w≤p<z}(1−g(p))⁻¹ ≤ K (log z/log w)^κ.
hypotheses: All endpoint choices are part of the definition: p=w is included and p=z is excluded. The predicate alone does not require g(p)<1; every sieve theorem requires 0≤g(p)<1 separately.
proofSteps: Take the finite product over primes below ceil z and filter by w≤p. Use real powers and the strictly positive logarithm of w.
acceptance: Do not infer this product-ratio condition from the logarithmic condition without controlling primes with g(p) near one.

nodes.title: Level of distribution of a sieve family
nodes.statement: HasSieveLevel(F,θ) for a fixed family F:real→BoundingSieve means θ>0, X_F(x)≥0 for all x≥2, and: for every A>0 there exist B>0,C>0,x₀≥2 such that for all x≥x₀, remainderMass(F(x), x^θ/(log x)^B)≤ C X_F(x)/(log x)^A.
hypotheses: F and θ are fixed before A is chosen. B,C,x₀ may depend on F,θ,A, not on the varying x. This is a weighted sieve-family predicate, not Maynard’s π-centred prime-distribution predicate.
proofSteps: Write out the order of quantifiers. Retain the absolute divisor sum, its strict cutoff and its mass-normalization remainder.
acceptance: An arbitrary coefficient level, a pointwise error without summed uniformity, or a negative approximate mass is not this condition.

nodes.title: Coefficient error controlled by remainder mass
nodes.statement: If L≥0, |c(d)|≤L on the divisors of P and c(d)=0 on every divisor d≥D, then s.errSum(c)≤L remainderMass(s,D).
hypotheses: s is a BoundingSieve; D is real and the cutoff is strict. This promotes the remainderMass API item used by Brun’s estimate.
proofSteps: Split the finite divisor sum by d<D. The complementary coefficients vanish. Bound each remaining nonnegative term by L|R_d| and factor the constant out.
acceptance: D≤1 forces every contributing coefficient to vanish; L=0 gives zero error.

sources.match: Exact coefficient-sensitive native form, without a claim that truncation proves distribution.

nodes.title: Finite tilted density Euler product
nodes.statement: For any real a and BoundingSieve s, Σ_{d|P} ν(d)d^a = ∏_{p|P}(1+ν(p)p^a).
hypotheses: P=s.prodPrimes is nonzero squarefree; all powers have positive natural bases, including d=1.
proofSteps: Use the native squarefree-divisor/subset correspondence. Multiplicativity of ν and real powers on positive products identify each subset term. Expand the finite product by choosing either 1 or ν(p)p^a at each prime.
acceptance: P=1 gives 1=1 for every a; a=0 gives Σν(d)=∏(1+ν(p)).

sources.match: The squarefree weighted analogue of the Euler-product expansion, derived on the existing carrier.

nodes.title: Weighted Rankin cutoff bound
nodes.statement: For x>0 and σ≥0, Σ_{d|P, d≤x} dν(d) ≤ x^σ ∏_{p|P}(1+ν(p)p^(1−σ)).
hypotheses: s is a BoundingSieve. The inclusive cutoff is explicit; x<1 gives an empty sum.
proofSteps: For d≤x compare d^σ≤x^σ, multiply by ν(d)d^(1−σ), and sum. Extend the sum by nonnegative terms and apply the finite Euler-moment identity with exponent 1−σ.
acceptance: σ=0 remains valid; x=1 retains the d=1 contribution; do not include d=0.

sources.match: Explicit finite weighted Rankin inequality; no smooth-number carrier or asymptotic estimate is redefined.

nodes.title: Weighted Rankin remainder-tail bound
nodes.statement: For x>0 and a≥0, Σ_{d|P, x<d} ν(d) ≤ x^(−a) ∏_{p|P}(1+ν(p)p^a).
hypotheses: s is a BoundingSieve; the tail is strict.
proofSteps: On the tail use 1≤(d/x)^a, retain nonnegative ν(d), and extend to all divisors. Apply the Euler-moment identity.
acceptance: At x=P the tail is empty; x<1 includes d=1; a=0 gives the full density sum as an upper bound.

sources.match: A finite Rankin replacement for the integral tail route, with all parameters and endpoints explicit.

nodes.title: Tilted Euler-product estimate from logarithmic dimension
nodes.statement: Fix a set P and function g, with κ>0,C≥0, nonnegative g(p) for selected primes and HasLogSieveDimension(P,g,κ,C). There exist K>0,z₀≥exp(2) such that for every z≥z₀, ∏_{p∈P,p prime,p≤z}(1+g(p)p^(1/log z)) ≤ K(log z)^κ.
hypotheses: All data P,g,κ,C are fixed before K,z₀ are chosen. The constants are independent of z and of every application population.
proofSteps: Set A(t)=Σ_{p≤t,p∈P}g(p)log p. Apply the native Abel formula on [2,z] to 1/log t, isolating p=2, to obtain Σg(p)≤κ log log z+O_{κ,C}(1). Its derivative is −1/(t(log t)²), integrable on this domain.
For α=1/log z and 2≤p≤z, use exp(u)−1≤exp(1)u for 0≤u=α log p≤1. Thus Σg(p)(p^α−1)≤exp(1)(κ+C/log z), uniformly bounded.

Extend the finite summand by zero off the selected primes before using Real.prod_one_add_le_exp_sum, whose input is globally nonnegative. Exponentiate the two bounds and absorb only fixed constants in K.
acceptance: The lower endpoint is at least exp(2), so 0<1−1/log z<1 in the cutoff applications. No Mertens theorem is required when the logarithmic condition is given.

sources.match: Explicit proof route for the Euler product used in the weighted Rankin exercise; the proof is specified, not implemented.

nodes.title: Dimension-controlled weighted divisor count
nodes.statement: For fixed data of log-dimension-euler-bound, there exist K>0,z₀≥exp(2) such that for every z≥z₀, every x>0 and every BoundingSieve s whose prime factors are exactly the selected primes p≤z and whose ν(p)=g(p), Σ_{d|P_s,d≤x}dν(d) ≤ K x(log z)^κ exp(−log x/log z).
hypotheses: Constants are uniform in x and s; all density data and dimension constants are fixed. This implies the strict-cutoff version of source Lemma 11.7.
proofSteps: Apply weighted Rankin with σ=1−1/log z, then bound its finite Euler product by the preceding theorem. Rewrite x^σ as x exp(−log x/log z).
acceptance: The inclusive cutoff is a stronger conclusion than the source’s d<x; x<1 gives an empty divisor sum.

sources.match: Same weighted sum with ω(d)=dν(d); preserves every uniform parameter.

nodes.title: Dimension-controlled divisor-density tail
nodes.statement: For the same fixed data there exist K>0,z₀≥exp(2) such that for every z≥z₀,x>0 and matching sieve s, Σ_{d|P_s,x<d}ν(d) ≤ K(log z)^κ exp(−log x/log z).
hypotheses: For a fixed L>0 replace x by Lx and absorb the bounded factor L^(−1/log z) in K.
proofSteps: Use weighted Rankin with a=1/log z and the tilted Euler-product estimate. This avoids integration of a divisor-count bound and so removes the extra log z loss of the source integral argument.
acceptance: This is a worker-derived stronger finite-tail estimate, not a quotation of the source’s (log z)^(κ+1) bound. No infinite divisor tail is asserted.

sources.match: The same finite tail, bounded directly by Rankin instead of the stated integral route.

nodes.title: Eratosthenes estimate with a justified mass and divisor cutoff
nodes.statement: Let x>0,c,M≥0 and 0<σ<1. If 0≤X≤Mx, |R_d|≤c dν(d) for divisors d≤x, and A_d=0 for divisors d>x, then |S−X∏_{p|P}(1−ν(p))|≤(c+M)x^σ∏_{p|P}(1+ν(p)p^(1−σ)).
hypotheses: s is the native BoundingSieve; A_d is its weighted multSum. The mass bound and the divisor cutoff are assumptions to prove in an application, never consequences of the residue-label representation.
proofSteps: Split the native absolute Legendre remainder into d≤x and d>x. Bound the first piece by c times the weighted prefix. On the tail, A_d=0 gives |R_d|=Xν(d); apply weighted Rankin with a=1−σ and X≤Mx. Combine the common Euler product.
With σ=1−1/log z and the dimension estimate obtain O_{fixed data,c,M}(x(log z)^κ exp(−log x/log z)).
acceptance: This conditional statement does not claim the exact advertised Theorem 11.9 under its weaker printed hypotheses, nor does it fix the two-residue cutoff gap E7 in the Brun application.

nodes.title: Brun combinatorial coefficients
nodes.statement: For squarefree P, y>1, β>1 and parity ε∈{0,1}, put λ_ε(d)=μ(d) if d|P and the decreasing prime factors p₁>⋯>p_r of d satisfy p_m<(y/(p₁⋯p_m))^(1/β) for every 1≤m≤r with m≡ε mod 2; otherwise put λ_ε(d)=0. Put λ⁺=λ₁ and λ⁻=λ₀. The empty prime list makes λ⁺(1)=λ⁻(1)=1.
hypotheses: Only positive divisors contribute. Prefix p₁⋯p_m includes p_m. Both coefficient systems retain every admissible prefix, not just divisors whose whole number of prime factors has one parity.
proofSteps: Sort the native finite prime-factor set decreasingly. Test the specified one-based prefix constraints, then use the existing Möbius coefficient with its sign. Define zero outside the positive divisor finset.
acceptance: For P=6,y=100,β=2, both systems retain d=1,2,3,6 and agree with μ on those divisors. For P=6,y=4,β=2,z=4, λ⁺ retains only 1 whereas λ⁻ retains 1,2,3; the first-order lower sum is negative on the two-prime obstruction.

Finite inclusion-exclusion leaves a sum of nonnegative first-failure contributions with the required parity sign. nodes.title: Dimension-controlled Brun main terms
nodes.statement: Let κ>0,K>1, β=9κ+1, u≥β,y>1,z=y^(1/u), all primes of P satisfy p<z, and g(p)=ν(p) on P and zero off P. Under HasProductSieveDimension(P,g,κ,K), with V=∏_{p|P}(1−ν(p)) and δ=exp(β−u)K^10, (1−δ)V ≤ mainSum(λ⁻) ≤ V ≤ mainSum(λ⁺) ≤ (1+δ)V.
hypotheses: P in the dimension predicate means the set of its prime factors. Strict prime-density bounds are supplied by BoundingSieve. The displayed non-strict inequalities include every degenerate empty-prime case.
proofSteps: Use the finite first-failure expansion with strict prime cutoffs and the last-prime left-limit product (E35): V⁺−V is the sum of odd-length failure masses, and V−V⁻ the sum of even-length failure masses. Each summand is nonnegative.

The prefix constraints give p_n≥z_n=z^(1−1/β)^n. Enlarge each summation domain; an ordered distinct-prime sum is at most the n-th power of the unrestricted prime sum divided by n!. The product-dimension bound controls V(z_n)/V(z); if z_n<2 use the identical empty-prime interval or the interval starting at 2.

Use the source’s b=9, a=exp(1+1/9)/9<exp(−1), its factorial bound n!≥exp(1)(n/exp(1))^n, and vanishing for n+β≤u. Sum the geometric tail to obtain δ. The lower main term has 1−δ, not the source display’s 1+δ (E33).
acceptance: δ may exceed one; then the lower bound can be negative and asserts no positive prime lower bound. Empty P gives V⁺=V⁻=V=1.

sources.match: Source estimate with the lower sign corrected from its first-failure proof.

nodes.title: Brun fundamental sieve estimate
nodes.statement: Under the Brun main-term hypotheses and X≥0, (1−δ)V X−remainderMass(s,y) ≤ S ≤ (1+δ)V X+remainderMass(s,y), where β=9κ+1,u≥β,z=y^(1/u), δ=exp(β−u)K^10.
hypotheses: This is the proved parameter range of this elementary combinatorial sieve. It is not a sharp beta-sieve theorem, a parity-breaking input or a Chen theorem.
proofSteps: Expand A_d=ν(d)X+R_d in both weighted brackets. The promoted modulus and support lemmas give |λ±|≤1 and support d<y. Apply the promoted remainder-mass error lemma, then multiply the main-term inequalities by nonnegative X.
acceptance: The range u≥9κ+1 and positivity of X are explicit. A positive sifted lower bound requires both δ<1 and a sufficiently small actual remainder mass.

nodes.title: From roughness to an almost-prime bound
nodes.statement: Let natural z≥2, n≠0 and k≥0. If every prime p dividing n satisfies z≤p and n<z^(k+1), then Nat.IsAtMostAlmostPrime(k,n).
hypotheses: Prime factors are counted with multiplicity. The upper bound is strict and the unit n=1 is allowed.
proofSteps: Every entry of the native prime factor list is at least z. Hence n, its product, is at least z raised to the list length Ω(n). If Ω(n)≥k+1, monotonicity of natural powers contradicts the strict upper bound. Use the existing at-most predicate, not the exact-k or distinct-factor predicate.
acceptance: n=8,z=2,k=2 violates the strict cutoff and has Ω=3 although it has only one distinct prime factor; n=1 gives Ω=0; n=0 is excluded.
